overview: Both cause common fungal skin and mucosal infections, but they belong to entirely different fungal groups with different habits.
genZNote: Keratin specialists versus the opportunist that goes anywhere warm and moist.

aspects.label: Overview / Core Definition
aspects.valueA: A group of molds (Trichophyton, Microsporum, Epidermophyton) that specifically digest keratin in skin, hair, and nails.
aspects.valueB: A genus of yeasts that are part of normal human flora but can overgrow to cause superficial or, rarely, systemic infection.

aspects.label: Morphology
aspects.valueA: Molds — grow as septate hyphae, producing characteristic macroconidia/microconidia.
aspects.valueB: Yeasts — round to oval budding cells, some species also form pseudohyphae.

aspects.label: Tissue Tropism
aspects.valueA: Restricted to keratinized, non-living tissue: skin, hair, nails.
aspects.valueB: Can affect skin folds, mucous membranes (oral thrush, vaginal candidiasis), and in immunocompromised hosts, deep tissue and bloodstream.

aspects.label: Source of Infection
aspects.valueA: Acquired from other infected people, animals, or soil (anthropophilic, zoophilic, geophilic species).
aspects.valueB: Endogenous — usually arises from the patient's own normal flora overgrowing.

aspects.label: Diagnostic Approach
aspects.valueA: KOH mount of skin/nail/hair scrapings showing branching hyphae; Wood's lamp fluorescence for some species.
aspects.valueB: KOH mount or Gram stain showing budding yeast with or without pseudohyphae; germ tube test for C. albicans.

aspects.label: Risk Factors
aspects.valueA: Warm, moist environments; skin-to-skin or fomite contact.
aspects.valueB: Antibiotic use, diabetes, immunosuppression, indwelling catheters.

aspects.label: Key Distinguishing Feature
aspects.valueA: Mold restricted to keratinized tissue, exogenous source.
aspects.valueB: Yeast that is normal flora and becomes opportunistic when the host is compromised.
